summary: The note is a news-style article reporting an apparent surge in solar tsunami (Moreton wave) activity observed by the Heliospheric Observational Center and its possible ecological consequences on Earth. It covers threats to the ozone layer, crops, phytoplankton and climate, and describes new monitoring satellites, predictive models, international summits, policy reviews and public awareness efforts.
one_line: Scientists report stronger, more frequent solar tsunamis and warn of risks to Earth's ozone layer, ecosystems and climate, prompting new monitoring and policy responses.
key_facts: On September 4, 2023, reports described an observatory dedicated to solar studies detecting the eruption of a solar tsunami.
Solar tsunamis are waves of hot plasma and magnetic fields rippling across the Sun's surface, caused by the release of vast magnetic energy during solar flares.
Dr. Eleanor Tao, lead solar physicist at the Heliospheric Observational Center (HOC), and colleagues have noticed stronger and more frequent solar tsunamis than ever before.
Solar tsunamis are also known as "Moreton waves" after their discoverer, Dr. Gail Moreton, and were once thought to be mainly of academic interest.
Dr. Tao says the waves traverse the Sun at speeds of up to 750,000 kilometers per hour.
Environmental chemist Dr. Marcus Zheng says intensified solar winds and increased ultraviolet radiation can result in ozone depletion, calling for immediate scientific inquiry and action.
Heightened UV through a compromised ozone layer could disrupt plant photosynthesis and reduce crop yields, affecting global food security.
Marine biologist Dr. Lina Nkomo warns that increased solar radiation can hinder phytoplankton growth, which underpins the marine food web and carbon sequestration in oceans.
Solar tsunamis do not directly cause climate change, but Dr. Tao says changes in solar radiation could speed up melting of ice caps and intensify weather phenomena.
On November 9, 2023, the HOC announced deployment of a new satellite array providing real-time data on solar tsunami activity.
Computational models are being developed to forecast the occurrence and risks of solar tsunamis.
Emergency summits have gathered experts from atmospheric chemistry to space weather, and governments are reviewing protocols, including revising climate models to include solar influences.
Proposed protections include reinforced satellite shielding and agricultural techniques that secure food sources against extreme UV exposure.
Educational initiatives for schools, communities and online platforms aim to raise public awareness and preparedness.
